---
title: "Advanced How"
---

::: {.lede}
Designing an RCT that produces reliable evidence. Behind every successful RCT are design
decisions made before the programme begins. Good randomization alone is not enough.
:::

## What makes an RCT credible?

[How](02-how.qmd) showed the process. This page shows what separates a strong RCT from a
weak one.

::: {.cards}
::: {.card-e}
[01]{.num}

#### Enough firms

Groups large enough to detect real impacts.
:::
::: {.card-e}
[02]{.num}

#### Comparable groups

A lottery that actually balanced the groups.
:::
::: {.card-e}
[03]{.num}

#### Reliable outcomes

Measures that capture what matters.
:::
::: {.card-e}
[04]{.num}

#### The right design

A setup matched to the policy question.
:::
:::

::: {.takeaway}
The sections below walk through each pillar, using SMART Romania as the test case.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="on">Enough firms</span><span class="sep">&rsaquo;</span><span>Comparable groups</span><span class="sep">&rsaquo;</span><span>Outcomes</span><span class="sep">&rsaquo;</span><span>Right design</span></div>
```

## Do I have enough firms?

Randomization only works if there are enough firms to detect meaningful differences.

::: {.compare}
::: {.col-e}
::: {.col-head}
Too few firms
:::
::: {.body}
```{=html}
<div class="dots" style="grid-template-columns:repeat(8,1fr);max-width:190px;margin-bottom:.8rem">
<span class="a"></span><span></span><span></span><span class="a"></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span>
<span></span><span></span><span class="a"></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span class="a"></span><span></span>
<span></span><span class="a"></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span>
</div>
```
Real impacts may go undetected: ordinary differences between firms drown out the
programme's effect.
:::
:::
::: {.col-e}
::: {.col-head}
Enough firms
:::
::: {.body}
```{=html}
<div class="dots" style="grid-template-columns:repeat(8,1fr);max-width:190px;margin-bottom:.8rem">
<span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span>
<span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span>
<span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span>
</div>
```
Real impacts become measurable: averages settle and the difference stands out.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.takeaway}
More firms do not make the lottery fairer; they make its answer visible.
:::

## Why sample size matters

How many firms are enough depends on what needs to be detected.

::: {.compare}
::: {.col-e}
::: {.col-head}
The size of the effect
:::
::: {.body}
**Small effect:** more firms needed.

**Large effect:** fewer firms needed.
:::
:::
::: {.col-e}
::: {.col-head}
The variation between firms
:::
::: {.body}
**High variation:** more firms needed.

**Low variation:** fewer firms needed.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.gold-panel}
Think of trying to hear a quiet voice in a noisy room: more background noise requires
more observations.
:::

## How is the required sample calculated?

Evaluators combine four ingredients into one required number, before the programme starts.

```{=html}
<figure class="fig-e">
<svg viewBox="0 0 680 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" role="img" aria-label="Expected effect, variation, confidence level and statistical power feed a power calculation, which returns the required sample size">
  <rect x="20" y="20" width="200" height="42" rx="5" fill="var(--dg-panel)" stroke="var(--dg-rule)"/>
  <text x="120" y="46" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12.5" font-weight="bold">Expected effect</text>

  <rect x="20" y="86" width="200" height="42" rx="5" fill="var(--dg-panel)" stroke="var(--dg-rule)"/>
  <text x="120" y="105" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12.5" font-weight="bold">Variation</text>
  <text x="120" y="120" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="10.5">(standard deviation)</text>

  <rect x="20" y="152" width="200" height="42" rx="5" fill="var(--dg-panel)" stroke="var(--dg-rule)"/>
  <text x="120" y="178" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12.5" font-weight="bold">Confidence level</text>

  <rect x="20" y="218" width="200" height="42" rx="5" fill="var(--dg-panel)" stroke="var(--dg-rule)"/>
  <text x="120" y="244" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12.5" font-weight="bold">Statistical power</text>

  <path d="M220 41 H250 V140 M220 107 H250 M220 173 H250 M220 239 H250 V140 M250 140 H272" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/>

  <rect x="272" y="110" width="176" height="60" rx="5" fill="var(--dg-accent)"/>
  <text x="360" y="135" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12.5" font-weight="bold">POWER CALCULATION</text>
  <text x="360" y="153" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="10.5">standard software does the math</text>

  <path d="M448 140 H478" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="1.5"/>

  <rect x="478" y="106" width="182" height="68" rx="5" fill="var(--dg-ink)"/>
  <text x="569" y="131" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-reverse)" font-size="12.5" font-weight="bold">Required sample size</text>
  <text x="569" y="150" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-reverse)" font-size="10.5">the minimum number of firms</text>
  <text x="569" y="164" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-reverse)" font-size="10.5">the study needs</text>
</svg>
</figure>
```

::: {.takeaway}
No formulas needed: calculators do this work. Links at the bottom of this page.
:::

## Was 1,038 enough?

Back to the case: how do evaluators know whether the SMART Romania pool was big enough?
Run the pool against the required sample from the power calculation, and do it before the
draw. If the pool falls short, grow the pool first (next section).

```{=html}
<figure class="fig-e">
<svg viewBox="0 0 680 190" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" role="img" aria-label="The pool of 1038 firms is checked against the required sample produced by the power calculation">
  <rect x="20" y="56" width="190" height="72" rx="6" fill="var(--dg-panel)" stroke="var(--dg-rule)"/>
  <text x="115" y="88" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="21" font-weight="bold">1,038</text>
  <text x="115" y="110" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="11.5">firms in the pool</text>

  <text x="278" y="97" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="13" font-weight="bold">checked</text>
  <text x="278" y="113" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="13" font-weight="bold">against</text>

  <path d="M338 92 H366" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="1.5"/>

  <rect x="366" y="56" width="294" height="72" rx="6" fill="var(--dg-accent-wash)"/>
  <text x="513" y="84" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12.5" font-weight="bold">Required sample</text>
  <text x="513" y="103" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="10.5">expected effect &rarr; power calculation &rarr; minimum firms</text>
</svg>
</figure>
```

```{=html}
<div class="case-band"><b>SMART Romania</b><span>&check; 1,038 eligible firms formed the randomized pool</span></div>
```

::: {.team-note}
**Data gap**
The baseline report contains no power calculation figures, so this section shows the logic
of the check without inventing numbers. Ask the evaluation team for the expected effect,
assumptions, and required sample, then add them here.
:::

## What if there are not enough firms?

The most common planning problem has practical fixes.

```{=html}
<div class="designs">
  <div class="d"><div>
    <h4>Increase outreach</h4>
    <p>More applications mean a larger pool. SMART Romania ran events in more than 20 cities.</p>
  </div></div>
  <div class="d"><div>
    <h4>Expand eligibility</h4>
    <p>Loosen the bar so more firms qualify.</p>
  </div></div>
  <div class="d"><div>
    <h4>Combine regions</h4>
    <p>Pool similar programmes or areas into one study.</p>
  </div></div>
  <div class="d"><div>
    <h4>Run a phase-in</h4>
    <p>Everyone participates; timing creates the comparison.</p>
  </div></div>
  <div class="d"><div>
    <h4>Target larger effects</h4>
    <p>Focus the programme where impacts are biggest.</p>
  </div></div>
  <div class="d"><div>
    <h4>Collect better baseline data</h4>
    <p>Good baselines reduce noise and cut the required sample.</p>
  </div></div>
</div>
```

Related on [How](02-how.qmd): the eligibility levers and phase-in designs.

```{=html}

```

## Did the lottery create comparable groups?

A lottery should produce two groups that look alike before the programme starts. Check it.

```{=html}
<figure class="fig-e">
<svg viewBox="0 0 680 320" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" role="img" aria-label="Illustrative balance check: treatment and comparison bars of near-equal length for firm age, revenue, employees and sector mix">
  <text x="20" y="26" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="10.5" letter-spacing="1.5" font-weight="bold">ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT REAL DATA</text>

  <text x="20" y="66" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">Firm age</text>
  <rect x="150" y="52" width="300" height="14" fill="var(--dg-ink)"/>
  <rect x="150" y="70" width="290" height="14" fill="var(--dg-accent)"/>

  <text x="20" y="130" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">Revenue</text>
  <rect x="150" y="116" width="340" height="14" fill="var(--dg-ink)"/>
  <rect x="150" y="134" width="352" height="14" fill="var(--dg-accent)"/>

  <text x="20" y="194" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">Employees</text>
  <rect x="150" y="180" width="260" height="14" fill="var(--dg-ink)"/>
  <rect x="150" y="198" width="268" height="14" fill="var(--dg-accent)"/>

  <text x="20" y="258" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">Sector mix</text>
  <rect x="150" y="244" width="310" height="14" fill="var(--dg-ink)"/>
  <rect x="150" y="262" width="302" height="14" fill="var(--dg-accent)"/>

  <rect x="150" y="296" width="11" height="11" fill="var(--dg-ink)"/>
  <text x="168" y="306" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="11.5">Treatment</text>
  <rect x="260" y="296" width="11" height="11" fill="var(--dg-accent)"/>
  <text x="278" y="306" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="11.5">Comparison</text>
</svg>
<figcaption>If the groups look the same before the programme starts, the lottery probably worked. Small differences are normal; large systematic ones are a warning sign.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

```{=html}
<div class="case-band"><b>SMART Romania</b><span>&check; The application survey collected the baseline data used for this check</span></div>
```

::: {.team-note}
**Data gap**
The balance bars are illustrative. The baseline report does not publish a treatment and
control balance table. Once the team shares the actual balance results, replace the bars
with the real characteristics and values, and remove the on-figure caveat.
:::

## Which outcomes should be measured?

An RCT is only as good as what it measures.

::: {.compare}
::: {.col-e}
::: {.col-head}
Good outcomes are
:::
::: {.body}
- **Relevant:** tied to the policy objective
- **Measurable:** data can actually be collected
- **Objective:** not dependent on opinion
- **Consistent:** collected the same way for every firm, every round
:::
:::
::: {.col-e}
::: {.col-head}
Measured in SMART Romania
:::
::: {.body}
- Digital adoption (DESI)
- Revenue
- Employment
- Productivity
:::
:::
:::

::: {.takeaway}
Fix the outcomes before the draw: choosing them afterwards invites cherry-picking.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span>Enough firms</span><span class="sep">&rsaquo;</span><span>Comparable groups</span><span class="sep">&rsaquo;</span><span>Outcomes</span><span class="sep">&rsaquo;</span><span class="on">Right design</span></div>
```

## What can go wrong?

Even a well-designed RCT must survive contact with reality.

::: {.caution}
**Attrition.** Firms drop out of surveys, and the groups stop matching.
:::

::: {.caution}
**Spillovers.** Comparison firms benefit anyway, and the measured difference shrinks.
:::

::: {.caution}
**Low take-up.** Treated firms never actually use the support.
:::

::: {.caution}
**Implementation problems.** The programme is delivered unevenly across firms.
:::

Monitoring answers all four: [Data Collection](05-data.qmd).

## When are the alternative designs worth it?

[How](02-how.qmd) introduced four alternative designs. The advanced question is when they
earn their extra sample and complexity.

::: {.cards}
::: {.card-e}
#### Multiple treatment arms

**Choose it when:** knowing which version works best matters more than sample size.
:::
::: {.card-e}
#### Phase-in

**Choose it when:** everyone must eventually receive the programme.
:::
::: {.card-e}
#### Randomized intensities

**Choose it when:** spillovers between firms or employees are the question.
:::
::: {.card-e}
#### Encouragement

**Choose it when:** access cannot be denied and take-up is the problem.
:::
:::

```{=html}
<div class="case-band"><b>SMART Romania</b><span>&check; A simple lottery was enough: one clear question, oversubscribed grants</span></div>
```

The mechanics of each design: [How](02-how.qmd).
